description: Build a predictive health monitoring software that gathers health indicators and enables astronauts to evaluate and act on the status of their health.
summary:
Baseline is health monitoring software for astronauts who are too far from Earth to wait for a doctor. On the way to Mars, a question to the flight surgeon can take up to 40 minutes to come back, so the crew has to notice problems alone. Today's monitors compare everyone with the same alarm limits, and a fit astronaut can drift a long way from their own normal without crossing one.

Baseline learns each astronaut's own normal from a two-minute daily check (camera pulse, reaction test, mood, sleep, symptoms, cuff and meter readings) plus wearable signals. It then answers three questions an ordinary monitor cannot: Is anything unusual for me? Is it me, the sensor, or the ship? Is my fix working? It warns before any alarm limit is crossed, ranks the likely cause, gives a plan, and tracks whether the plan worked.

We tested the idea on real Inspiration4 crew blood data from NASA's Open Science Data Repository and on 1,000 simulated astronauts. It runs offline in a browser as a single file.
details:
Try it: https://ishanroutray.github.io/baseline/

The problem

On a trip to Mars, a question to the flight surgeon can take up to 40 minutes to come back. The crew has to catch health problems on their own. The monitors they have compare every person with the same alarm limits, and those limits are built for the average person. A fit astronaut can change a lot and still look "normal". We saw this in real data: after the Inspiration4 flight, the standard lab range flagged none of the four crew, even though all four had moved outside their own usual values.

What Baseline does

Baseline learns what is normal for you, then watches for you drifting away from it.

Each day the astronaut does a two-minute check: pulse measured through the camera, a tap reaction test, mood, sleep, symptoms, and cuff and meter readings. Wearables fill in the rest, 19 signals in total. Days 8 to 30 of the mission set that person's baseline. After that, Baseline scores five body systems (immune, heart and circulation, bone and muscle, sleep and mood, food and metabolism) by how far several signals have moved together. A warning needs two days in a row, so one odd reading does not set it off.

The astronaut sees one status, a clickable body figure, the signals behind any warning, a 14-day forecast, the most likely cause, and a plan. If it gets serious, Baseline builds a 4 kB summary to send to the ground. Every measurement has a short explanation of how it is taken in space and why it matters. It works for a space station, a Moon base, Mars transit and a Mars base, and tracks radiation dose against NASA's career limit.

What is new

Most monitors ask one question: is this number past the limit? Baseline asks three.

1. Is this unusual for me? It can warn while every single reading is still inside the limits.

2. Is it me, the sensor, or the ship? If one signal jumps alone, it is probably the sensor. If the whole crew shifts on the same days and CO2 or workload is high, it is probably the ship. Your crewmates work as your control group.

3. Is my fix working? You start a plan and Baseline shows what your body did next to what it predicted.

So a number is never just "high" or "fine". Baseline says whether it is unusual for you, what is most likely causing it, and whether what you did about it helped. The statistics behind this are well known. Putting the three together for a crew that cannot call a doctor is the part we have not seen in other projects.

How we tested it

Real astronauts. Using Inspiration4 blood counts from NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSD-569), each person's own pre-flight range flagged red blood cell size the day after landing for 4 of 4 crew. The standard lab range flagged 0 of 4.

Simulated crews. We built a simulator where every astronaut is a different person, and gave them hidden problems: immune activation, missed exercise, sleep and mood decline, overwork, and under-eating. We set the alert levels on one group of missions and tested on 250 missions that were never used for tuning (1,000 astronauts). Baseline caught 87.6% of the problems. With the same false-alarm rate, Hotelling T-squared caught 62.4% and a 3-sigma rule caught 55%. Fixed limits caught 11.7%. Half of Baseline's alerts came within 9 days of the problem starting. About 1 in 5,000 healthy days gave a false alert. It ranked the right cause first 84.6% of the time, where guessing would get 12.5%.

Sensors and plans. Baseline caught 85% of sensor faults, usually within 3 days, and cut the false health alerts they cause from 22.5% to 10.8%. When the simulated astronaut started the plan at the first warning, days spent at alert level over the next month dropped from 12 to 0.5 for the immune case.

Real wearables. On an open COVID-19 wearable dataset, it warned in 4 of 9 infections with no false warnings in the comparison group. That is a modest result and we are reporting it as it is.

What went wrong

Our first detector looked perfect on one scripted mission. When we ran it on 100 healthy missions, it raised a false alert in 90 of them. We fixed four things: the baseline keeps learning on quiet days and freezes when a drift starts, the math accounts for today's reading depending on yesterday's, each body system has its own alert level, and an alert needs two days. After that, 2% of healthy crew ever saw an alert.

What it cannot do yet

The crew in the app is simulated, and we designed the simulated problems ourselves, so those numbers show the method works under our assumptions, not that it would score the same on a real crew. The real-astronaut test is four people on a three-day flight. The camera pulse has not been checked against a medical device. Baseline does not diagnose anything. The next step would be data from analog missions like HERA and CHAPEA.

How we built it

HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no outside libraries. We did that on purpose: a crew on the way to Mars has no usable internet, so the app cannot depend on downloading anything. The whole thing fits in one 175 KB file that runs from the ship's own computer. We used Node.js for the calibration and benchmark scripts, Python for the two real-data tests, and GitHub Pages for hosting. Every number here can be reproduced from the scripts in the repository. We chose statistics we can explain over a black-box model because an astronaut has a few weeks of their own data, not millions of rows, and because a crew will only trust a warning if they can see what it is based on.
